The goal of '''S-estimators''' is to have a simple [[Robust statistics#Breakdown point|high-breakdown]] [[Linear regression|regression estimator]], which share the flexibility and nice asymptotic properties of [[M-estimators]]. The name "S-estimators" was chosen as they are based on estimators of scale.

We will consider estimators of scale defined by a function <math>\rho</math>, which satisfy

* R1 – <math>\rho</math> is symmetric, [[Differentiable function|continuously differentiable]] and <math>\rho(0)=0</math>.
* R2 – there exists <math>c > 0</math> such that <math>\rho</math> is strictly increasing on <math>[c, \infty]  </math>

For any sample  <math>\{r_1, ..., r_n\}</math>  of real numbers, we define the scale estimate  <math>s(r_1, ..., r_n)</math> as the solution of

<math display="inline" id="eq: s-scale">\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \rho(r_i/s) = K</math>,

where <math>K</math> is the [[Expected value|expectation value]] of <math>\rho
</math> for a [[Normal distribution|standard normal distribution]]. (If there are more solutions to the above equation, then we take the one with the smallest solution for s; if there is no solution, then we put  <math>s(r_1, ..., r_n)=0</math>  .)

Definition:

Let <math>(x_1, y_1), ..., (x_n, y_n)</math> be a sample of regression data with p-dimensional <math>x_i</math>. For each vector <math>\theta
</math>, we obtain residuals <math>s(r_1(\theta),..., r_n(\theta))</math> by solving the equation of scale above, where <math>\rho</math> satisfy R1 and R2. The S-estimator <math>\hat\theta</math> is defined by

<math>\hat\theta = \min_\theta \, s(r_1(\theta),...,  r_n(\theta))</math>

and the final scale estimator <math>\hat \sigma</math> is then

<math>\hat\sigma = s(r_1(\hat\theta), ..., r_n(\hat\theta))</math>.<ref>P. Rousseeuw and V. Yohai, Robust Regression by Means of S-estimators, from the book: Robust and nonlinear time series analysis, pages 256–272, 1984</ref>
